description: Interactive element definitions for IL-26 (every module >= 2 elements). All datasets fictional and original. Renderer shell built separately.

tasks.prompt: List each company and month with the natural log of users, so exponential growth plots as a straight line.
tasks.hint: Use the LN() function on the users column and alias it ln_users.

tasks.prompt: Compute the month-over-month growth factor per company: users divided by the prior month's users (use LAG).
tasks.starterSQL:
SELECT company, month, users
FROM growth_metrics;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT company, month,
  users / LAG(users) OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY month) AS growth_factor
FROM growth_metrics
ORDER BY company, month;
tasks.hint: LAG(users) OVER (PARTITION BY company ORDER BY month) gives the prior month; the first month per company yields NULL.

tasks.prompt: Show companies with April users above 2000, with LOG10(users) for a log-scale chart axis.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT company, LOG10(users) AS log10_users
FROM growth_metrics
WHERE month = '2026-04' AND users > 2000
ORDER BY company;
tasks.hint: Filter month = '2026-04' and users > 2000; all three companies qualify.

tasks.prompt: Total sales per store: a summation over days, grouped by store.
tasks.starterSQL:
SELECT store, amount
FROM daily_sales;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT store, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
FROM daily_sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;
tasks.hint: SUM(amount) with GROUP BY store gives Harbor 1930, Lakeshore 1355, Riverside 2540.

tasks.prompt: Grand total across all stores and days: the double summation.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUM(amount) AS grand_total
FROM daily_sales;
tasks.hint: Drop the GROUP BY to collapse everything to one row: 5825.

tasks.prompt: For each store, the sum of squared daily amounts: a building block of variance.
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT store, SUM(amount * amount) AS sum_of_squares
FROM daily_sales
GROUP BY store
ORDER BY store;
tasks.hint: Square inside the SUM: SUM(amount * amount).

tasks.prompt: UNION: customers who are enterprise OR signed up in 2026-02, one row per customer.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise'
UNION
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE signup_month = '2026-02'
ORDER BY name;
tasks.hint: UNION deduplicates: 5 enterprise + 3 February signups - 1 overlap (Cara) = 7.

tasks.prompt: INTERSECT: customers who are BOTH enterprise AND signed up in 2026-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.hint: Only Cara satisfies both conditions.

tasks.prompt: EXCEPT: enterprise customers who did NOT sign up in 2026-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE segment = 'enterprise'
EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE signup_month = '2026-02'
ORDER BY name;
tasks.hint: Removes Cara from the 5 enterprise customers: Ada, Fay, Ivy, Leo.

tasks.prompt: Average, minimum, and maximum salary per department.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT dept, salary FROM employee_comp;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT dept,
  AVG(salary) AS avg_salary,
  MIN(salary) AS min_salary,
  MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employee_comp
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
tasks.hint: AVG, MIN, MAX with GROUP BY dept.

tasks.prompt: Departments with more than 3 employees, with headcount.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employee_comp GROUP BY dept;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employee_comp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
ORDER BY dept;
tasks.hint: HAVING filters after grouping: Engineering (4) and Support (4).

tasks.prompt: The overall standard deviation of salary: one number describing spread.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee_comp;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT STDDEV(salary) AS salary_stddev
FROM employee_comp;
tasks.hint: STDDEV (or STDDEV_POP) aggregates the whole table to one row.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Discrete calculus: running totals and differences

tasks.prompt: Running total of temperature: a discrete integral, via a windowed SUM ordered by time.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts,
  SUM(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM sensor_readings
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: SUM() OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) accumulates; the explicit frame makes the intent clear.

tasks.prompt: Hour-over-hour temperature change: a discrete derivative, via LAG.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts,
  temp_c - LAG(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) AS hourly_change
FROM sensor_readings
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: Subtract the LAG value; the first row has no prior reading so its change is NULL.

tasks.prompt: Flag the hours where temperature rose more than 1.0 degree versus the prior hour.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT reading_ts, temp_c FROM sensor_readings;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT reading_ts, temp_c
FROM (
  SELECT reading_ts, temp_c,
    temp_c - LAG(temp_c) OVER (ORDER BY reading_ts) AS chg
  FROM sensor_readings
) t
WHERE chg > 1.0
ORDER BY reading_ts;
tasks.hint: Compute the change in a subquery, then filter: 10:00 (+1.3), 11:00 (+1.8), 12:00 (+1.5).

tasks.prompt: Rank orders within each region by amount and return the top order per region.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT region, customer, amount FROM orders ORDER BY region, amount DESC;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT region, customer, amount
FROM (
  SELECT region, customer, amount,
    RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rnk
  FROM orders
) t
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY region;
tasks.hint: RANK (not ROW_NUMBER) keeps ties: East has two orders at 5100, so 4 rows return.

tasks.prompt: Running total of amount per region, ordered by order date, with an explicit frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT region, order_date, amount FROM orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT region, order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
FROM orders
ORDER BY region, order_date;
tasks.hint: PARTITION BY region restarts the total per region; the frame clause states the window explicitly.

tasks.prompt: Month-over-month change per customer: aggregate to monthly totals in a CTE, then LAG.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT customer, amount FROM orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT customer, SUBSTRING(order_date, 1, 7) AS ym, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer, SUBSTRING(order_date, 1, 7)
),
lagged AS (
  SELECT customer, ym, total,
    LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ym) AS prev
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT customer, ym, total, total - prev AS mom_change
FROM lagged
WHERE prev IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY customer, ym;
tasks.hint: The CTE collapses to customer-months; LAG gives the prior month; 8 customer-months have a predecessor.

tasks.prompt: Customers whose lifetime total exceeds their region's average customer total (two CTEs).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT customer, region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer, region;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH cust_tot AS (
  SELECT customer, region, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders GROUP BY customer, region
),
region_avg AS (
  SELECT region, AVG(total) AS avg_total
  FROM cust_tot GROUP BY region
)
SELECT c.customer, c.region, c.total
FROM cust_tot c JOIN region_avg r ON c.region = r.region
WHERE c.total > r.avg_total
ORDER BY c.customer;
tasks.hint: Beta (West), Echo and Foxtrot (East), Gamma and Helios (Central) clear their regional averages.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Channel performance: rates and variability in SQL

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate and average revenue per channel.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, converted, revenue FROM site_sessions;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel,
  SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
  AVG(revenue) AS avg_revenue
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: A rate is a mean of 0/1 flags: SUM(converted)*1.0/COUNT(*).

tasks.prompt: Revenue variability per channel: standard deviation and maximum.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, AVG(revenue) FROM site_sessions GROUP BY channel;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel,
  STDDEV(revenue) AS revenue_stddev,
  MAX(revenue) AS max_revenue
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: STDDEV next to the mean tells you whether the average is stable or noisy.

tasks.prompt: Channels with at least 5 sessions and a conversion rate above 0.5.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT channel, COUNT(*) FROM site_sessions GROUP BY channel;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT channel, SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate
FROM site_sessions
GROUP BY channel
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5 AND SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) > 0.5
ORDER BY channel;
tasks.hint: HAVING filters groups: organic (3/5) and paid (3/5) qualify; referral has only 4 sessions.

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate and average minutes per variant, with each variant's lift versus the overall average rate.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, AVG(minutes) FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH rates AS (
  SELECT variant,
    SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
    AVG(minutes) AS avg_minutes
  FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant
)
SELECT variant, conv_rate, avg_minutes,
  conv_rate - AVG(conv_rate) OVER () AS lift_vs_avg
FROM rates
ORDER BY variant;
tasks.hint: AVG() OVER () with no partition computes the grand mean across the two variant rows.

tasks.prompt: Sample size per variant: are the arms balanced?
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, COUNT(*) FROM ab_users GROUP BY variant;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT variant, COUNT(*) AS n_users
FROM ab_users
GROUP BY variant
ORDER BY variant;
tasks.hint: 6 and 6: balanced. Unbalanced arms are the first thing to check before trusting a readout.

tasks.prompt: Conversion rate by variant AND new-vs-returning segment: does the effect hold in both?
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT variant, is_new, converted FROM ab_users;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT variant, is_new,
  SUM(converted) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS conv_rate,
  COUNT(*) AS n
FROM ab_users
GROUP BY variant, is_new
ORDER BY is_new, variant;
tasks.hint: New users: 0.667 both arms (no effect). Returning: 0.333 vs 0.667 (effect concentrated here).

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Grain checks on a sales fact table

tasks.prompt: Revenue by category: qty * unit_price summed at fact grain.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, qty, unit_price FROM sales_lines;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT category, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS revenue
FROM sales_lines
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
tasks.hint: Multiply inside the SUM: Electronics 994, Tools 600, Accessories 139.86.

tasks.prompt: Grain violations: order_id + product pairs appearing more than once.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, product FROM sales_lines;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, product, COUNT(*) AS line_count
FROM sales_lines
GROUP BY order_id, product
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1003/Widget A and o1010/Gadget Y are double-counted: the fact grain is broken there.

tasks.prompt: Dimension sanity: distinct customers and distinct orders in one row.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_lines;
tasks.hint: 7 customers, 11 orders: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) measures dimension cardinality.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Staging cleanup: dedupe, clean, incremental filter

tasks.prompt: Deduplicate: one row per (user_id, event_ts, event_type), keeping the lowest event_id.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, event_type, amount
FROM (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, event_ts, event_type ORDER BY event_id) AS rn
  FROM stg_events
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY event_ts;
tasks.hint: Two duplicate pairs (e1/e3, e2/e10) collapse: 14 rows become 12.

tasks.prompt: Clean amounts: purchase events only, with NULL amounts replaced by 0.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events WHERE event_type = 'purchase';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, COALESCE(amount, 0) AS clean_amount
FROM stg_events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
ORDER BY event_id;
tasks.hint: COALESCE(amount, 0) handles the NULL on e5; views and the refund are excluded.

tasks.prompt: Incremental load: only events newer than the watermark 2026-09-02.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM stg_events;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT event_id, event_ts
FROM stg_events
WHERE event_ts > '2026-09-02'
ORDER BY event_ts;
tasks.hint: The watermark excludes everything through 2026-09-02: 9 rows remain.

tasks.prompt: Monthly category totals: the year-month grain a Tableau extract would carry.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT txn_date, category, amount FROM retail_txns;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category,
  SUM(amount) AS total
FROM retail_txns
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
ORDER BY ym, category;
tasks.hint: Year-month plus category gives 9 groups across the six months.

tasks.prompt: Best month per category by total (RANK over the monthly totals).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, SUM(amount) FROM retail_txns GROUP BY category;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM retail_txns
  GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
)
SELECT ym, category, total
FROM (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total DESC) AS rnk FROM m) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
tasks.hint: One row per category: Outdoor peaks 2026-01 (380), Fitness peaks 2026-03 (140)... verify against the CTE.

tasks.prompt: Rolling 3-month total per category with an explicit window frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT category, txn_date, amount FROM retail_txns;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7) AS ym, category, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM retail_txns
  GROUP BY SUBSTRING(txn_date, 1, 7), category
)
SELECT ym, category,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY ym
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_3mo
FROM m
ORDER BY category, ym;
tasks.hint: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW builds the trailing window; early months sum fewer rows.

tasks.prompt: NULL counts for email and phone in a single row.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM crm_contacts;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN email IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS email_nulls,
  SUM(CASE WHEN phone IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS phone_nulls
FROM crm_contacts;
tasks.hint: SUM over a CASE expression counts NULLs: 1 email, 2 phones.

tasks.prompt: Duplicate emails: values appearing more than once, with counts.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT email FROM crm_contacts;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM crm_contacts
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY email;
tasks.hint: ana@northwind.com and ben@beacon.io each appear twice.

tasks.prompt: Invalid emails: values not matching a basic '%@%.%' pattern.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT contact_id, email FROM crm_contacts;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT contact_id, email
FROM crm_contacts
WHERE email IS NOT NULL AND email NOT LIKE '%@%.%'
ORDER BY contact_id;
tasks.hint: 'cara AT beacon.io' and 'gus@copperline' fail the pattern; NULLs are excluded first.

tasks.prompt: 5xx error rate per hour: errors divided by total requests, grouped by hour.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT ts, status FROM web_logs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUBSTRING(ts, 1, 13) AS hr,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS err_rate
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(ts, 1, 13)
ORDER BY hr;
tasks.hint: Four distinct hours; the first three each have one 5xx in four requests (0.25).

tasks.prompt: Top 3 paths by total bytes served.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT path, bytes FROM web_logs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT path, SUM(bytes) AS total_bytes
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY path
ORDER BY total_bytes DESC
LIMIT 3;

tasks.prompt: Distinct client IPs per day: a proxy for daily active users.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT client_ip, ts FROM web_logs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT SUBSTRING(ts, 1, 10) AS day,
  COUNT(DISTINCT client_ip) AS distinct_ips
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY SUBSTRING(ts, 1, 10)
ORDER BY day;

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Versioned tables: current state and change history

tasks.prompt: Current state: the latest version of each order (what a MERGE target holds).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, customer, amount, updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT *,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY version DESC) AS rn
  FROM delta_orders
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: One row per order_id: o1 through o8.

tasks.prompt: Orders with more than one version: the change-history audit.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, version FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS versions, MAX(version) AS latest_version
FROM delta_orders
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1 (2 versions), o3 (3), o5 (2).

tasks.prompt: Orders whose latest amount differs from their first version: real changes, not no-op rewrites.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT order_id, amount, version FROM delta_orders;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT order_id,
    MIN(CASE WHEN version = 1 THEN amount END) AS first_amt,
    MAX(CASE WHEN version = (SELECT MAX(version) FROM delta_orders d2 WHERE d2.order_id = delta_orders.order_id) THEN amount END) AS last_amt
  FROM delta_orders GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT order_id FROM v WHERE first_amt <> last_amt ORDER BY order_id;
tasks.hint: o1 (1000 to 1100) and o3 (800 to 900); o5 rewrote the same 1500.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Job-search analytics on your applications tracker

tasks.prompt: Funnel counts by stage: where every application stands.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT stage FROM applications;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT stage, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM applications
GROUP BY stage
ORDER BY n DESC;
tasks.hint: Six stages: applied 5, rejected 3, screening 2, interview 2, offer 1, ghosted 1.

tasks.prompt: Response rate by source: share of applications reaching screening or beyond.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT source, stage FROM applications;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT source,
  SUM(CASE WHEN stage IN ('screening','interview','offer') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS response_rate
FROM applications
GROUP BY source
ORDER BY response_rate DESC;
tasks.hint: company site 0.50, Indeed 0.333, referral 0.333, LinkedIn 0.286.

tasks.prompt: Stale applications: still 'applied' more than 21 days after applying (today 2026-10-07).
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT company, applied_date, stage FROM applications;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT company, applied_date
FROM applications
WHERE stage = 'applied'
  AND applied_date < DATE '2026-10-07' - INTERVAL '21 days'
ORDER BY applied_date;
tasks.hint: Harbor Health, Beacon Insurance, Prairie Credit Union, Alloy Systems; Ironwood is only 19 days old.

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Interview-pressure SQL: CTE chains, frames, ties

tasks.prompt: Three-CTE chain: daily net per account, then account totals, then the top 2 accounts by net flow.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account;

tasks.prompt: 3-day moving average of daily net flow per account, with an explicit ROWS frame.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) AS net
  FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date
)
SELECT account, txn_date,
  AVG(net) OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY txn_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma_3d
FROM daily
ORDER BY account, txn_date;
tasks.hint: Daily grain: a100 has 6 days, a200 has 4, a300 has 4: 14 rows.

tasks.prompt: Top 2 withdrawal amounts per account, keeping ties: DENSE_RANK, not ROW_NUMBER.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, amount FROM bank_txns WHERE txn_type = 'withdrawal';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT account, amount
FROM (
  SELECT account, amount,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY ABS(amount) DESC) AS dr
  FROM bank_txns WHERE txn_type = 'withdrawal'
) t
WHERE dr <= 2
ORDER BY account, ABS(amount) DESC;
tasks.hint: a100 keeps both -200 rows (tie for rank 1) plus -120; a200 and a300 contribute one row each.

tasks.prompt: For each account, the day with the largest net outflow; ties broken by earliest date.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT account, txn_date, SUM(amount) AS net
  FROM bank_txns GROUP BY account, txn_date
)
SELECT account, txn_date, net
FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account ORDER BY net ASC, txn_date ASC) AS rn
  FROM daily
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY account;

sqlPlaygrounds.title: Objects, links, and properties in SQL

tasks.prompt: Build the link table: origin to destination pairs with shipment counts and total weight.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT origin, destination FROM shipments;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT origin, destination,
  COUNT(*) AS shipments,
  SUM(weight_kg) AS total_kg
FROM shipments
GROUP BY origin, destination
ORDER BY shipments DESC;
tasks.hint: Six distinct lanes; Chicago Hub to Detroit Depot is the busiest with 4 shipments.

tasks.prompt: Late-delivery rate per carrier: delivered after the promised date.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT carrier, delivery_date, promised_date FROM shipments;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT carrier,
  SUM(CASE WHEN delivery_date > promised_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS late_rate,
  COUNT(*) AS n
FROM shipments
GROUP BY carrier
ORDER BY carrier;
tasks.hint: Meridian 1/7 late, BlueArrow 2/5 late.

tasks.prompt: Shipments whose origin handles at least 4 shipments: the hub-and-spoke core.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT origin, COUNT(*) FROM shipments GROUP BY origin;
tasks.hint: Only Chicago Hub clears the bar, with 6 shipments.

tasks.prompt: Trial balance per account: total debits, total credits, and the difference.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, side, SUM(amount) FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY account, side;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT account,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS debits,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'credit' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS credits,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) AS difference
FROM ledger_entries
GROUP BY account
ORDER BY account;
tasks.hint: Five accounts; 1002 and 1005 show nonzero differences that need investigation.

tasks.prompt: Breaks: (account, side, amount, value_date) tuples in core but missing from custody.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core';
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT account, side, amount, value_date
FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
EXCEPT
SELECT account, side, amount, value_date
FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
ORDER BY account;
tasks.hint: Four one-sided breaks: 1002 credit 12000, 1003 debit 7500, 1004 debit 3000, 1005 credit 9000.

tasks.prompt: Aging: breaks (either direction) older than 2 days as of 2026-09-05.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT * FROM ledger_entries;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH breaks AS (
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  UNION
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount, value_date FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
)
SELECT * FROM breaks
WHERE value_date < DATE '2026-09-05' - INTERVAL '2 days'
ORDER BY value_date;
tasks.hint: Only the 2026-08-20 pair for account 1004 is older than 2 days: both its sides.

tasks.prompt: Net break exposure per account: unmatched debits positive, unmatched credits negative; show nonzero.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH breaks AS (
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  UNION
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'custody'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT account, side, amount FROM ledger_entries WHERE source_system = 'core'
)
SELECT account,
  SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) AS net_exposure
FROM breaks
GROUP BY account
HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN side = 'debit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) <> 0
ORDER BY account;
tasks.hint: 1002 nets to -12000 and 1005 to -9000; 1003 and 1004 offset to zero.

tasks.prompt: Completeness: the 3 daily reports across 4 days; find missing report-days.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT DISTINCT report_name FROM report_runs;
tasks.solutionSQL:
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT SUBSTRING(run_ts, 1, 10) AS day FROM report_runs
),
reps AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT report_name FROM report_runs
  WHERE report_name IN ('CCAR Summary','Liquidity Snapshot','Risk Positions')
),
expected AS (
  SELECT day, report_name FROM days CROSS JOIN reps
)
SELECT e.day, e.report_name
FROM expected e
LEFT JOIN report_runs r
  ON SUBSTRING(r.run_ts, 1, 10) = e.day AND r.report_name = e.report_name
WHERE r.run_id IS NULL;
tasks.hint: Risk Positions never ran on 2026-09-04: the one gap in 12 expected report-days.

tasks.prompt: Checksum changes: runs whose checksum differs from that report's prior run.
tasks.starterSQL: SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum FROM report_runs ORDER BY report_name, run_ts;
tasks.solutionSQL:
SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum
FROM (
  SELECT report_name, run_ts, checksum,
    LAG(checksum) OVER (PARTITION BY report_name ORDER BY run_ts) AS prev_checksum

branchingScenarios.title: Interview pressure: the Monty Hall question

start.text: The interviewer leans in: three doors, one prize. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the prize is, opens door 3 to reveal nothing. Stay with door 1 or switch to door 2?

choices.label: Switch to door 2
choices.feedback: Right instinct: the host's knowledge concentrates probability.

choices.label: Stay with door 1; it is 50/50 now
choices.feedback: Tempting, but the host did not choose randomly.

switch.text: Good. The interviewer pushes: prove it. Why isn't it 50/50 between the two remaining doors?

choices.label: The host's action moves the 2/3 chance onto door 2
choices.feedback: Exactly: your door keeps its 1/3; the other unopened door inherits the rest.

choices.label: Switching just feels luckier
choices.feedback: Weak: interviewers want the mechanism, not the vibe.

stay.text: The interviewer raises an eyebrow: walk me through the probability, step by step.

choices.label: Reconsider: the host gave me information by avoiding the prize
choices.feedback: Good recovery: a non-random reveal is information.

choices.label: Two doors remain, so it must be 50/50
choices.feedback: This ignores that the host's choice was constrained by knowledge.

end.text: Debrief: Monty Hall tests whether you update on non-random information. State the mechanism (1/3 stays, 2/3 concentrates), then generalize: always ask whether new information was generated randomly or selectively.

branchingScenarios.title: Incident response: the PII dashboard request

start.text: Marketing wants customer email addresses added to the shared campaign dashboard for spot-checking. Forty people can see it, including contractors.

choices.label: Add the emails; the stakeholder owns the requirement
choices.feedback: Risky: stakeholder ownership does not transfer privacy risk.

choices.label: Propose a hashed customer ID for spot-checks instead
choices.feedback: Strong: solve the underlying need without exposing identifiers.

choices.label: Add them but restrict the dashboard to the marketing team
choices.feedback: Better, but restriction is a speed bump, not a control.

pressure.text: Marketing escalates: legal supposedly said it is fine, but you have nothing in writing.

choices.label: Require the approval in writing before changing anything
choices.feedback: Correct: verbal legal clearance is not clearance.

choices.label: Proceed on their verbal assurance
choices.feedback: If this goes wrong, the decision trail points at you.

good.text: The hashed ID works. Now they ask for phone numbers too, same dashboard.

choices.label: Apply the same rule: no direct identifiers on shared surfaces
choices.feedback: Consistent: the principle does not change with the column.

choices.label: Phones are less sensitive; allow it
choices.feedback: Phones are direct identifiers and enable the same harm.

partial.text: Restricted to 8 people. A contractor screenshots the dashboard and emails it outside the company.

choices.label: Treat it as an incident: contain, notify, rotate what you can
choices.feedback: Right: restriction failed, so incident process takes over.

choices.label: It was only 8 people; handle it quietly
choices.feedback: Quiet handling hides the blast radius from the people who own the risk.

end.text: Debrief: default-deny on direct identifiers in shared surfaces, propose safer alternatives that meet the real need, get approvals in writing, and treat restriction as mitigation, never as the control.

start.text: Your manager asks you to report active users with a definition that counts anyone who opened the app once. It doubles the number right before the board meeting.

choices.label: Use their definition; it is their call
choices.feedback: The number will carry your name when the board asks questions.

choices.label: Show both definitions side by side, methodology noted
choices.feedback: Transparent: the board sees the choice instead of inheriting it.

choices.label: Refuse outright and escalate above your manager
choices.feedback: Disproportionate as a first move; negotiation usually works.

comply.text: The board celebrates. Next quarter the definition quietly reverts and growth goes negative.

choices.label: Accept it as a lesson about ownership
choices.feedback: The lesson is real, but the credibility damage is too.

choices.label: Document your objection now, after the fact
choices.feedback: Late documentation protects no one; the moment was before publication.

honest.text: Your manager is annoyed but the board appreciates the clarity and picks the stricter definition going forward.

choices.label: Hold the line on methodology notes in every deck
choices.feedback: This is the senior habit: definitions travel with numbers, always.

choices.label: Let the manager present it alone next time
choices.feedback: Withdrawing avoids conflict but abandons the standard you just set.

refuse.text: Escalation burns trust with your manager over a disagreement that had a middle path.

choices.label: Apologize and propose the side-by-side approach
choices.feedback: Recovery is possible: lead with the workable alternative.

choices.label: Stand your ground on principle
choices.feedback: Principle matters, but so does proportionality; pick battles with no compromise path.

end.text: Debrief: never publish a number whose definition you would not defend in front of the board. Side-by-side with methodology is the standard move; escalation is the last resort, not the first.

start.text: A director Slacks you: can you pull some data on churn? No context, no deadline, no decision attached.

choices.label: Start querying immediately to show speed
choices.feedback: Speed without direction usually produces the wrong artifact.

choices.label: Ask what decision this will inform: the 5 whys
choices.feedback: The senior move: scope follows the decision, not the data.

choices.label: Send last quarter's churn deck; it is probably fine
choices.feedback: Stale analysis presented as fresh is a quiet credibility risk.

why.text: Three whys in, the truth surfaces: the CFO is deciding whether to fund a retention program and needs churn by segment, this week.

choices.label: Scope it: segments, timeframe, one-page readout by Friday
choices.feedback: A scoped commitment beats an open-ended promise every time.

choices.label: Promise the full analysis by tomorrow morning
choices.feedback: Overpromising sets up the exact failure you were trying to avoid.

rush.text: You deliver a 40-tab workbook. They needed one number for a meeting in an hour.

choices.label: Extract the one number and send it now
choices.feedback: Salvageable, but the rework was avoidable with one question.

choices.label: Defend the workbook's thoroughness
choices.feedback: Thoroughness that misses the decision is just latency.

deck.text: The deck's churn definition changed two quarters ago; the numbers are not comparable.

choices.label: Recall it and rebuild on the current definition
choices.feedback: Painful but correct; shipping known-stale numbers is worse.

choices.label: Add a footnote about the definition change
choices.feedback: A footnote does not fix a misleading headline number.

end.text: Debrief: vague requests get questions, not queries. Find the decision, the audience, and the deadline first; then commit to a scoped deliverable you can actually hit.

branchingScenarios.title: Stakeholder management: saying no with alternatives

start.text: Sales wants a forecast, Product wants funnel analysis, Finance wants a variance report. All three say by Friday. You are one analyst.

choices.label: Work the weekend and do all three
choices.feedback: Heroics scale once; expectations scale forever.

choices.label: Rank the three by business impact with the requesters, then sequence
choices.feedback: The professional play: make the tradeoff visible and shared.

choices.label: Do the easiest one well and quietly drop the others
choices.feedback: Silent drops surface at the worst possible moment.

sequence.text: The three leads agree: the forecast unblocks a pricing decision, so it goes first; the variance report can wait until Tuesday.

choices.label: Confirm the sequence in writing with dates
choices.feedback: Written sequencing is what makes the agreement stick.

choices.label: Keep it verbal; everyone seemed aligned
choices.feedback: Alignment without a record evaporates by Thursday.

burnout.text: You ship all three, exhausted. Next week brings four requests.

choices.label: Set the sequencing norm now, while the win is fresh
choices.feedback: Convert the heroics into a process before the pattern hardens.

choices.label: Accept this as the new normal
choices.feedback: Unsustainable pace degrades the quality they are praising.

drop.text: Finance discovers the missing variance report during close.

choices.label: Own it and deliver a rush version
choices.feedback: Accountability helps, but the trust dent remains.

choices.label: Blame competing priorities
choices.feedback: Blame without a sequencing process just spreads the frustration.

end.text: Debrief: no is a complete answer when it comes with a ranked alternative. Make tradeoffs explicit, get them agreed in writing, and never let silent drops or heroics become the operating model.

branchingScenarios.title: Tooling judgment: R or Python for this task?

start.text: Your team is Python-first, but the certificate project template is in R and the stakeholder's legacy report is an R Markdown file that still runs monthly.

choices.label: Rewrite everything in Python immediately
choices.feedback: Purity has a cost: rewrites introduce risk with no stakeholder benefit.

choices.label: Keep R for the legacy report; use Python for new work
choices.feedback: Pragmatic: match the tool to the job and the team.

choices.label: Do the whole project in R to match the template
choices.feedback: The template is a starting point, not a constraint.

pragmatic.text: The legacy report keeps running untouched; your new analysis ships in Python and the team can review it.

choices.label: Document the boundary: what stays in R and why
choices.feedback: Explicit boundaries prevent the next person from re-litigating this.

choices.label: Quietly plan to migrate the R report later
choices.feedback: A migration needs a reason; if it runs fine, leave it.

rewrite.text: The rewrite takes two weeks and introduces a subtle aggregation difference nobody catches for a month.

choices.label: Add reconciliation checks between old and new outputs
choices.feedback: If you must rewrite, prove equivalence before switching.

choices.label: Ship it; the logic was straightforward
choices.feedback: Straightforward logic still deserves a parity check.

ronly.text: Nobody on the team can review your R code, and onboarding the next analyst gets harder.

choices.label: Add thorough comments to compensate
choices.feedback: Comments help, but they do not replace reviewable code.

choices.label: Offer to teach the team R
choices.feedback: A big ask to solve a problem you created.

end.text: Debrief: tool choice is a team decision, not a personal preference. Keep working systems working, write new work in the team's stack, and document the boundary.

branchingScenarios.title: Certification strategy: planning the Google certificate

start.text: You have 8 weeks for the Google Data Analytics certificate. It covers spreadsheets, SQL, R, and a capstone, but your SQL is already strong.

choices.label: Study everything equally: two weeks per area
choices.feedback: Equal time ignores your starting position.

choices.label: Skim SQL, double down on R and the capstone case study
choices.feedback: Allocate to the gap: strengths need maintenance, weaknesses need reps.

choices.label: Skip straight to the capstone; you learn by doing
choices.feedback: The capstone assumes the foundations; gaps surface mid-project.

focus.text: R clicks by week 5 and the capstone has a solid week of polish time.

choices.label: Do timed practice on the weakest R topics
choices.feedback: Targeted reps beat re-reading chapters.

choices.label: Re-read the SQL material anyway for completeness
choices.feedback: Completeness is the enemy of the schedule; trust the skim.

equal.text: Week 7 arrives with R still shaky and the capstone untouched.

choices.label: Reallocate remaining time to R and the capstone
choices.feedback: Late reallocation is better than none, but the plan should have done this.

choices.label: Push through on the original schedule
choices.feedback: Sunk-cost scheduling: the plan serves you, not the reverse.

capstone.text: Mid-capstone you hit R data-cleaning tasks the coursework would have made routine.

choices.label: Pause the capstone and backfill the R foundations
choices.feedback: Correct call: foundations first, even mid-project.

choices.label: Work around the gaps with spreadsheets
choices.feedback: Workarounds become the permanent, fragile solution.

end.text: Debrief: study plans allocate time to gaps, not to comfort. Skim strengths, drill weaknesses, and protect capstone time like a deadline.

start.text: Monday 8 AM: the executive dashboard shows revenue down 40% overnight. The pipeline ran green.

choices.label: Alert everyone that revenue has collapsed
choices.feedback: A green pipeline with a 40% move smells like data, not business.

choices.label: Check source row counts before raising any alarm
choices.feedback: Measure first: row counts separate data incidents from real ones.

choices.label: Re-run the pipeline; green runs cannot be wrong
choices.feedback: Re-running a green pipeline reproduces the same wrong result.

triage.text: The source feed has 60% fewer rows than Friday: the vendor changed the export format over the weekend.

choices.label: Pin a data-quality notice on the dashboard and page the vendor contact
choices.feedback: Textbook: contain the misinformation, then fix the cause.

choices.label: Quietly patch the parser and backfill
choices.feedback: A silent fix leaves no audit trail and the notice never goes up.

panic.text: Leadership spends the morning modeling layoffs before anyone checks the feed.

choices.label: Own the false alarm publicly
choices.feedback: Owning it is right, but the trust cost was avoidable.

choices.label: Blame the pipeline's green status
choices.feedback: The pipeline did its job; the verification step was yours.

rerun.text: Same result, one hour lost, and the dashboard still shows the 40% drop.

choices.label: Now check the source row counts
choices.feedback: You arrive at triage an hour late; the notice should have been up.

choices.label: Escalate to engineering as a pipeline bug
choices.feedback: Escalating a data issue as a pipeline bug misdirects the fix.

end.text: Debrief: a green run is not a correct run. Check row counts and distributions first, contain bad numbers with a visible notice, fix with an audit trail, and never let executives act on unverified moves.

branchingScenarios.title: Certification strategy: the IBM certificate path

start.text: The IBM Data Analyst certificate covers Python, SQL, and visualization, but you already hold strong pandas skills from the Python module.

choices.label: Take every course in order, front to back
choices.feedback: Linear paths waste your scarcest resource: study hours.

choices.label: Test out of the Python sections via the practice assessments, then focus on the gaps
choices.feedback: Assess first: prove the strength, then spend time where it counts.

choices.label: Skip the certificate; your portfolio proves the skills
choices.feedback: Portfolios prove skill; certificates prove baseline to HR filters.

assess.text: You place out of two Python courses and find the SQL-for-analysis section genuinely new.

choices.label: Finish the SQL sections and the capstone project
choices.feedback: Targeted completion: the credential plus actual new skill.

choices.label: Also redo the Python courses for the certificate of completion
choices.feedback: Completionism over learning: the hours do not buy you anything.

linear.text: Week 4: you are re-learning groupby for the third time while the capstone waits.

choices.label: Switch to assessment-first now
choices.feedback: Pivoting mid-course recovers the schedule.

choices.label: Finish what you started
choices.feedback: Finishing a misallocated plan is just slower misallocation.

skip.text: A recruiter screen asks for a baseline credential and moves on to the next candidate.

choices.label: Reconsider: the certificate is cheap insurance for HR filters
choices.feedback: Pragmatic: credentials open doors portfolios cannot.

choices.label: Double down on portfolio only
choices.feedback: A defensible strategy, but you accept the filter risk knowingly.

end.text: Debrief: assess before you study, spend hours on gaps, and treat entry-level certificates as HR-filter insurance rather than learning endpoints.

branchingScenarios.title: Interview scenario: SQL on the whiteboard

start.text: The interviewer asks for top-2 customers per region by revenue, live on the whiteboard, narrating as you go. Your mind goes blank on window functions.

choices.label: Freeze and stare at the board
choices.feedback: Silence reads as stuck; narration buys thinking time.

choices.label: Narrate your plan first: aggregate, then rank, then filter
choices.feedback: Structure first: interviewers grade the plan as much as the syntax.

choices.label: Write a GROUP BY and hope the ranking sorts itself out
choices.feedback: Hoping the query self-assembles is not a strategy.

narrate.text: You outline: CTE for customer-region totals, RANK() partitioned by region, filter rank <= 2. The interviewer nods.

choices.label: Write the CTE carefully, checking each clause aloud
choices.feedback: Deliberate and narrated beats fast and silent.

choices.label: Rush the syntax to show speed
choices.feedback: Speed without checking is how ties and off-by-ones slip in.

freeze.text: Ten seconds of silence. The interviewer offers: want to talk through the approach first?

choices.label: Take the lifeline: describe the plan in words
choices.feedback: Good recovery: the plan is gradable even without syntax.

choices.label: Decline and keep staring
choices.feedback: Declining help signals worse than needing it.

hope.text: The GROUP BY is correct but there is no ranking; the interviewer asks how you limit to top 2 per region.

choices.label: Pivot to the window-function plan now
choices.feedback: Recoverable: name the missing piece explicitly.

choices.label: Suggest LIMIT 2
choices.feedback: LIMIT 2 gives two rows total, not two per region.

end.text: Debrief: narrate the plan before the syntax, build in CTE-sized steps you can verify aloud, and treat interviewer prompts as lifelines, not judgments.

branchingScenarios.title: Product sense: defining the right metric

start.text: Interview prompt: this analytics product's weekly active users are flat, but the team feels engagement is growing. What do you measure?

choices.label: Report WAU anyway; it is the standard metric
choices.feedback: Standards are defaults, not answers.

choices.label: Decompose engagement: sessions per active user, depth per session, feature mix
choices.feedback: Decomposition finds the growth the headline hides.

choices.label: Survey users about whether they feel engaged
choices.feedback: Feelings are data, but lagging and noisy for this question.

decompose.text: Sessions per user are up 20%; a new workflow feature drives it. The interviewer asks: is that good?

choices.label: Check retention of the new behavior before celebrating
choices.feedback: Senior answer: intensity without retention is a sugar rush.

choices.label: Declare victory: engagement is growing
choices.feedback: Premature: you have not ruled out novelty effects.

wau.text: Flat WAU, flat story. The interviewer waits.

choices.label: Pivot to decomposition now
choices.feedback: Better late: the structured answer was always available.

choices.label: Argue WAU is the only metric that matters
choices.feedback: Doubling down on the flat metric ends the discussion.

survey.text: Users say they love it. The interviewer asks how you would verify behaviorally.

choices.label: Pair the survey with session-depth and return-rate data
choices.feedback: Attitude plus behavior is the complete answer.

choices.label: Trust the survey; users know best
choices.feedback: Stated preference without revealed preference is half the picture.

end.text: Debrief: when the headline metric is flat, decompose before you conclude. Intensity, depth, and retention together tell the engagement story; any one alone can mislead.

start.text: You must model a logistics network: shipments move between facilities via carriers, and analysts need late-delivery rates by lane and carrier. Where do you start?

choices.label: List tables first: shipments, facilities, carriers
choices.feedback: Tables before concepts risks modeling the source system, not the domain.

choices.label: Name the objects, their properties, and the links between them
choices.feedback: Ontology first: objects, properties, links; tables follow.

choices.label: Ask engineering what the source schema looks like
choices.feedback: Source-first modeling inherits source-system quirks.

ontology.text: Objects: Shipment, Facility, Carrier. Links: Shipment runs Facility-to-Facility, is carried by Carrier. Properties: weights, dates, promised vs delivered.

choices.label: Derive the lane link table and late-rate measures from the links
choices.feedback: The model directly yields the analysis: lanes are links, late rates are link properties.

choices.label: Add every attribute anyone might ever want
choices.feedback: Attribute hoarding without use cases bloats the model.

tables.text: You build three tables mirroring the operational database, and late-rate logic gets tangled in joins.

choices.label: Refactor around the lane concept explicitly
choices.feedback: Recovery: name the domain concept and remodel.

choices.label: Push through with complex SQL
choices.feedback: Complexity compounds; the model debt grows.

source.text: The source schema has shipment legs split across two systems with different IDs.

choices.label: Model the domain linkage independently of source keys
choices.feedback: Right: the ontology needs its own identity resolution.

choices.label: Pick one system's IDs as canonical
choices.feedback: Inherits the chosen system's blind spots.

end.text: Debrief: model the domain before the database. Name objects, properties, and links; let the analysis you need (lanes, late rates) validate the model.

start.text: Morning reconciliation: account 1002 shows a 12,000 credit in core banking with no matching custody entry. The report goes to risk in two hours.

choices.label: Adjust the custody side to match; the amounts must tie
choices.feedback: Plugging breaks is how reconciliation fraud starts; never adjust to force a tie.

choices.label: Quarantine the break, age it, and report it as an open item
choices.feedback: The control mindset: breaks are reported, not hidden.

choices.label: Wait: maybe the custody feed is just late
choices.feedback: Possible, but hope is not a control.

quarantine.text: The break is logged, aged, and flagged. Risk asks: could it be a timing difference?

choices.label: Show the value-date matching rule and the feed cutoff times
choices.feedback: Evidence over opinion: the matching rule decides.

choices.label: Agree it is probably timing and close it
choices.feedback: Closing on probably defeats the purpose of the control.

plug.text: The report ties. Next week audit finds the manual adjustment with no ticket.

choices.label: Document it retroactively
choices.feedback: Retroactive documentation does not restore the control.

choices.label: Reverse the adjustment and reopen the break
choices.feedback: The only clean path, but the trust damage is done.

wait.text: Two hours pass; the custody feed arrives and the entry is genuinely missing, not late.

choices.label: Quarantine and report it now
choices.feedback: Late triage is still triage, but the report went out unflagged.

choices.label: Roll it into tomorrow's reconciliation
choices.feedback: Deferring a known break is a choice with a paper trail.

end.text: Debrief: reconciliation breaks are reported and aged, never plugged. Timing differences are decided by matching rules and cutoff evidence, not by optimism.

start.text: Internal audit finds three report runs last month with no approver recorded, including one CCAR Summary whose checksum changed between runs. The finding draft lands on your desk.

choices.label: Dispute it: the reports were correct
choices.feedback: Correctness is not the finding; the missing control is.

choices.label: Accept it and propose a fix: approval gates before publication
choices.feedback: Own the gap: controls, not correctness, are the issue.

choices.label: Blame the tooling: the approval field was optional
choices.feedback: Tooling explains; it does not absolve the process owner.

accept.text: You propose: reports cannot publish without a recorded approver, and checksum changes trigger re-approval.

choices.label: Add the rule to the runbook and backfill the missing approvals
choices.feedback: Complete: preventive control plus remediation of the gap.

choices.label: Implement the gate but skip the backfill
choices.feedback: The historical gap stays open for the next audit.

dispute.text: Audit shows the finding is about control design, not report accuracy. Disputing it escalates the severity.

choices.label: Concede and propose the fix
choices.feedback: Recovery is possible once you address the actual finding.

choices.label: Escalate to your VP
choices.feedback: Escalating a valid finding burns capital for nothing.

blame.text: The tooling was indeed optional-by-default, but your team owned the process.

choices.label: Fix the process and the tooling default
choices.feedback: Both layers: make the control unavoidable.

choices.label: Ask IT to lock the field
choices.feedback: A technical fix without a process owner still drifts.

end.text: Debrief: audit findings about controls are answered with controls. Accept the gap, make the control unavoidable, remediate history, and document it.

branchingScenarios.title: Day in the life: pipeline incident triage

start.text: 9:12 AM: the 8 AM sales mart refresh failed. The CEO's dashboard is stale and the 10 AM revenue huddle is at risk. PagerDuty names you.

choices.label: Restart the job immediately
choices.feedback: Restarting before diagnosis can corrupt partial state.

choices.label: Check the failure logs and the last successful run's watermark
choices.feedback: Diagnose first: logs, then watermark, then blast radius.

choices.label: Tell the CEO the dashboard will be late
choices.feedback: Notification matters, but lead with facts, not just delay.

diagnose.text: The load step failed on a schema change in the source: a new column broke the insert. The watermark is intact at 7 AM.

choices.label: Pin a stale-data notice, fix the schema mapping, rerun from the watermark
choices.feedback: Textbook triage: contain, fix forward, rerun cleanly.

choices.label: Drop the new column and rerun
choices.feedback: Dropping data silently changes the mart's contract.

restart.text: The restart fails the same way, and now there are two overlapping partial loads.

choices.label: Stop, diagnose the schema error, clean the partial load
choices.feedback: Recovery costs more than the diagnosis would have.

choices.label: Restart once more; third time lucky
choices.feedback: Hope is not a runbook.

notify.text: The CEO appreciates the heads-up and asks what happened and when it will be fixed.

choices.label: Diagnose first, then report with a timeline
choices.feedback: Right order: facts, then communication.

choices.label: Promise it will be fixed by 10
choices.feedback: Promising before diagnosing sets up a second failure.

end.text: Debrief: triage is diagnose, contain, communicate, fix. Never restart blind, never silently change the data contract, and always report with a timeline grounded in the diagnosis.

start.text: The CFO asks: what will Q4 revenue be? Your model says 4.2M, but the prediction interval is 3.1M to 5.3M and a key input just changed.

choices.label: Answer 4.2M confidently
choices.feedback: A point estimate without uncertainty is a promise you cannot keep.

choices.label: Give the range, the key drivers, and what would move it
choices.feedback: Ranges plus drivers: the executive-grade answer.

choices.label: Say the model is too uncertain to answer
choices.feedback: Abdicating the question abandons your seat at the table.

range.text: The CFO asks which driver matters most and what you recommend.

choices.label: Name the top driver, quantify its swing, recommend a hedge
choices.feedback: Decision-ready: uncertainty translated into action.

choices.label: List all twelve drivers equally
choices.feedback: Equal weighting is no weighting; prioritize.

point.text: Q4 lands at 3.4M. The CFO remembers your confident 4.2M.

choices.label: Show the interval you had and explain the miss
choices.feedback: Honest post-mortem, but the confident point already spent trust.

choices.label: Blame the changed input
choices.feedback: The input change was knowable when you answered.

dodge.text: The CFO turns to someone willing to give a number.

choices.label: Re-enter with the range and drivers
choices.feedback: Better late: a ranged answer beats no answer.

choices.label: Stay out of it
choices.feedback: Silence cedes the analysis to whoever speaks.

end.text: Debrief: executives need ranges, not points; drivers, not dumps; and recommendations, not abdication. Uncertainty communicated well builds more trust than false precision.

start.text: You have time for three portfolio projects. Candidates: a churn analysis, an ETL pipeline, a dashboard, a pricing experiment, and a data-quality audit.

choices.label: Pick the three you find most fun
choices.feedback: Fun optimizes for you; hiring managers optimize for evidence.

choices.label: Cover three hiring signals: analysis, engineering, communication
choices.feedback: Portfolio as evidence: one project per signal.

choices.label: Do all five superficially to look productive
choices.feedback: Breadth without depth reads as tutorial-following.

cover.text: You pick churn analysis, the ETL pipeline, and the dashboard. Each needs a README that explains the business question.

choices.label: Write decision-focused READMEs: question, method, result, next step
choices.feedback: Hiring managers skim for judgment, not code volume.

choices.label: Let the code speak for itself
choices.feedback: Code without narrative forces the reader to guess the point.

fun.text: Three fun projects, all exploratory analysis, no engineering or communication evidence.

choices.label: Add the missing signals with project number four
choices.feedback: Recovery: rebalance toward the signals.

choices.label: Ship them as-is
choices.feedback: A portfolio of one signal looks like one skill.

five.text: Five thin projects; every README says work in progress.

choices.label: Cut to three and finish them properly
choices.feedback: Finished beats numerous, every time.

choices.label: Ship all five
choices.feedback: Unfinished work signals unfinished thinking.

end.text: Debrief: a portfolio is evidence, not activity. Cover analysis, engineering, and communication; finish fewer projects completely; narrate the business decision in every README.

branchingScenarios.title: Dashboard portfolio: what hiring managers want

start.text: You are choosing which dashboards to feature. One is visually stunning but answers no business question; another is plain but drove a pricing decision.

choices.label: Feature the stunning one; visuals get clicks
choices.feedback: Clicks are not interviews; hiring managers test for decisions.

choices.label: Feature the plain one and explain the decision it drove
choices.feedback: Impact over aesthetics: the story is the product.

choices.label: Feature both and let viewers decide
choices.feedback: Curation is the skill; abdication is not.

plain.text: You write up the pricing decision: the analysis, the recommendation, the outcome.

choices.label: Include the messy middle: the wrong turns and what you learned
choices.feedback: Process transparency is senior signal.

choices.label: Present only the polished final view
choices.feedback: Polish without process looks like a template.

pretty.text: In an interview, the hiring manager asks what decision it informed. Silence.

choices.label: Pivot to the plain dashboard's story
choices.feedback: The story was always the asset.

choices.label: Talk about the design techniques
choices.feedback: Technique without purpose does not survive the question.

both.text: The portfolio page is crowded and the strong piece gets lost.

choices.label: Curate down to the decision-driven work
choices.feedback: Editing is part of the craft.

choices.label: Keep everything; more is more
choices.feedback: More dilutes; curation concentrates.

end.text: Debrief: feature dashboards that drove decisions, narrate the business question and outcome, show your working, and curate ruthlessly.

start.text: Your capstone idea: predict customer churn, build the pipeline, the model, the dashboard, and a real-time API. Six weeks.

choices.label: Build it all; ambition impresses
choices.feedback: Ambition without scoping produces five half-systems.

choices.label: Cut to the decision: which customers to save, and how the business acts on it
choices.feedback: Scope to the decision: prediction serving retention action.

choices.label: Start building and see how far you get
choices.feedback: Drift discovers scope by exhaustion.

cut.text: Scoped: batch churn scores, a pipeline, and a dashboard the retention team can act on. The API becomes a documented next step.

choices.label: Define done: scored, explained, dashboarded, reproducible
choices.feedback: A crisp definition of done is what makes six weeks enough.

choices.label: Keep the API as a stretch goal
choices.feedback: Stretch goals quietly become commitments; document, do not promise.

all.text: Week 4: the pipeline works, the model is unvalidated, the dashboard is a sketch, the API is a README.

choices.label: Cut scope now and finish the core
choices.feedback: Late scoping still beats shipping nothing finished.

choices.label: Push harder on all five
choices.feedback: More effort on five fronts finishes none.

drift.text: Week 3 and you are tuning hyperparameters for a model with no pipeline feeding it.

choices.label: Stop and write the blueprint: decision, data, deliverables
choices.feedback: The blueprint should have come first; second-best is now.

choices.label: Keep tuning; the model is the impressive part
choices.feedback: A model with no pipeline is a notebook, not a capstone.

end.text: Debrief: scope the capstone to a business decision, define done crisply, cut ruthlessly, and let stretch goals live in documentation, not in promises.

start.text: The take-home arrives Friday 5 PM, due Monday 9 AM: analyze a messy 50k-row dataset and recommend whether to expand to a new market. No other guidance.

choices.label: Start coding immediately; time is short
choices.feedback: Coding before framing burns the scarcest hours on the wrong question.

choices.label: Spend Friday night framing: the decision, the analyses, the risks
choices.feedback: Framing first: an hour of structure saves ten of rework.

choices.label: Email asking for clarification and wait
choices.feedback: Clarification is good; waiting all weekend is not.

frame.text: Framed: market sizing, unit economics under three scenarios, and the data-quality caveats. Saturday is execution.

choices.label: Timebox each analysis and reserve Sunday for the writeup
choices.feedback: The writeup is the deliverable; analysis without narrative does not get hired.

choices.label: Chase every interesting thread in the data
choices.feedback: Interesting is not the same as decision-relevant.

code.text: Sunday night: twelve charts, no recommendation, and a data-quality issue you noticed too late.

choices.label: Write the recommendation from what you have, flagging the caveat
choices.feedback: Salvageable if the caveat is front and center.

choices.label: Pull an all-nighter to redo it
choices.feedback: Exhaustion degrades the judgment the case is testing.

choices.label: Proceed with stated assumptions, documented
choices.feedback: Documented assumptions beat waiting.

choices.label: Keep waiting; guessing wrong is worse
choices.feedback: Waiting consumes the weekend; assumptions are gradable.

end.text: Debrief: take-homes grade judgment under time pressure. Frame the decision first, timebox ruthlessly, document assumptions, and reserve real time for the narrative: the recommendation is the product.

start.text: Final round: tell me about a time your analysis was wrong. You have a real story: a forecast that missed because of a data bug you caught late.

choices.label: Tell the polished version where you were the hero
choices.feedback: Polished stories dodge the question; interviewers notice.

choices.label: Tell it straight: the miss, the cause, what changed in your process
choices.feedback: STAR with a real failure and a process fix is the strongest answer.

choices.label: Say you have never been wrong
choices.feedback: Nobody believes it, and it ends the trust.

straight.text: They follow up: what would you do differently with the same data today?

choices.label: Name the specific check you added: source row-count alerts before modeling
choices.feedback: Concrete process change beats abstract lessons.

choices.label: Say you would be more careful
choices.feedback: Vague; the process fix was the whole point.

polish.text: The interviewer probes the timeline; the polish cracks.

choices.label: Drop the polish and tell the real version
choices.feedback: Honesty under pressure recovers well.

choices.label: Hold the polished line
choices.feedback: Doubling down on spin is memorable in the wrong way.

deny.text: Awkward silence. The interviewer moves on, unimpressed.

choices.label: Reopen it later with the real story
choices.feedback: Late honesty beats none, barely.

choices.label: Let it go
choices.feedback: The impression stands.

end.text: Debrief: behavioral rounds reward honest failure stories with process fixes. STAR format, real miss, specific change. Never polish, never deny.

start.text: Day 1 of your 90-day plan: SQL is solid, Python is decent, statistics is shaky, and you have zero portfolio pieces. Certifications and applications both compete for time.

choices.label: Apply to jobs immediately; you can learn on the job
choices.feedback: Applying without evidence burns first impressions you cannot remake.

choices.label: Sequence: stats foundations, then portfolio proof, then targeted applications
choices.feedback: Foundations, then proof, then applications: each phase funds the next.

choices.label: Collect three certifications before applying anywhere
choices.feedback: Certificates without proof of work stall at the portfolio review.

sequence.text: Day 30: statistics is functional and project one is underway. A recruiter asks for your portfolio link.

choices.label: Send project one with a clear README, noting two more in progress
choices.feedback: Honest momentum beats a finished facade.

choices.label: Say the portfolio is coming soon
choices.feedback: Soon without evidence is just a promise.

apply.text: Two rejections cite lack of demonstrated analysis work.

choices.label: Pause applications and build the proof
choices.feedback: The market gave you the feedback; act on it.

choices.label: Apply wider
choices.feedback: Volume does not fix an evidence gap.

certs.text: Day 60: three certificates, still no portfolio. Applications ask for work samples.

choices.label: Convert cert projects into portfolio pieces now
choices.feedback: Late but effective: proof over paper.

choices.label: Add a fourth certificate
choices.feedback: Diminishing returns accelerate from here.

end.text: Debrief: sequence the 90 days so each phase funds the next: shore up the shakiest foundation, build proof of work, then apply with evidence. Certificates support the story; they are not the story.
